## Writing & Coding == Thinking

> If writing down your ideas always makes them more precise and more complete, then no one who hasn't written about a topic has fully formed ideas about it. And someone who never writes has no fully formed ideas about anything nontrivial. ~ @graham:2022

&nbsp;

> Writing is thinking. To write well is to think clearly. That's why it's so hard. ~ @mccullough:2002

::: {.notes}

:::

::: {style="margin-top:0px;"}
# There are *no* shortcuts to thinking and learning.
::: 

## So Why Use a LLM to Learn to Code?

Many students use LLMs to *write* their code for three reasons:

1. They are available at all hours as a personal tutor and advisor.
2. They write better code, more quickly than a learner.
3. They can employ advanced techniques right away.

. . . 

::: {.callout-tip}
### Pro-Tip
Only *one* of these is a good reason.
:::

::: {.notes}

These accelerate code production, but there are significant doubts about code quality.

:::

## So Why Use a LLM to Learn to Write?

Many students use LLMs to *write* their assessments for three reasons:

1. They are available at all hours as a personal tutor and advisor.
2. They write better sentences, more quickly than a learner.
3. They draw on a wider range of sources and styles than a learner.

. . . 

::: {.callout-tip}
### Pro-Tip
Only *one* of these is a good reason.
:::

::: {.notes}

These accelerate word production, but there are significant doubts about quality.

:::

## Don't Take My Word for It {.smaller}

> Using AI in education is like using a forklift at the gym. The weights do not actually need to be moved from place to place. That is not the work. The work is what happens within you. ~ [Seemingly a conversation on YouTube? ](https://youtu.be/08NuUbcgT9Q?si=jbT_sWOBSDjrKdg4)

::: {.notes}
O the gym analogy... Students don't come to uni to learn to write essays. Even those that come to learn (not just 'get a degree') often see learning as an accumulation of knowledge rather than the strengthening of a skill.
:::

. . . 

From @Richmond:2025:

> Research has long shown that meaningfully processing new pieces of information -- in other words, thinking hard about something -- is vital for retaining that information in your long-term memory...

. . . 

> Moreover, the impact of AI tools appears to differ between groups of students. Younger students and those with lower prior attainment were more likely to use it in ways that are detrimental to their learning...

::: {.notes}

The takeaway: These classes are not the work. The work is what happens within you.

Critical thinking, problem solving, the idea that the world is knowable. That is the work happening with you.

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### LLMs as co-authors

Using ChatGPT as your co-*pilot* is not the same as using ChatGPT as your co-*author*. See the module's [AI policy](../assessments/index.qmd#use-of-ai) for what is and isn't permitted in the assessments.

:::


::: {.notes}

The people making the *best* use of LLMs are people who already know how to code or write.

:::

## A 'Safe' Prompt {.scrollable .smaller}

New this year: a [draft LLM session prompt](../ref/PROMPT.md).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

print('::: {style="font-style:fixed;"}')

from pathlib import Path
with open(Path('../ref/PROMPT.md'), 'r') as f:
    prompt = f.readlines()
printing = False
for p in prompt:
    if p.startswith('```markdown'):
        printing = True
    
    elif p.startswith('```'):
        printing = False
        next
    
    elif printing == True:
        print(p)

print(':::')
```
